summary: Medicine Bow Peak WY ground lookout: wooden cabin about 1909, later a cupola building; staffed 1910s-30s; gone; old remains in the saddle below the summit.

facts.design: Small wooden ground cabin built about 1909, later replaced by a larger structure with a cupola
facts.status_note: Listed as gone by the Forest Fire Lookout Association and firelookout.com; a bare caption on Forest Lookouts reads 'Burned by the Forest Service' without a date or structure; a 2022 blog describes old remains in the saddle below the summit

access.note: Site lies in Medicine Bow National Forest and a 2022 hiking blog describes hiking up from Sugarloaf Campground; no closure notice found, but no current visitor rules found either

visit.trail_note: Remains of the old lookout sit in the saddle below the summit, not on top; a sign on the route points out to them (2022 blog)

events.note: Small wooden ground cabin built on the site about 1909 (FFLOS gives circa 1909)
Contract awarded in July 1909 for a telephone line between Centennial and the peak
Fred J. Miller recommended for appointment as lookout in July 1910; by 1912 described as the ranger who occupied the post during the summer and fall
Lightning-caused fire on the lookout point, reported by Fred Miller; covered about an acre before it was put out
Newspaper item reports a new observatory built on the peak with glass on all sides
Lorraine Lindsley of Centennial took the lookout post; she resigned effective October 9, 1921 to return to the University of Wyoming
Late September 1921: smoke that Miss Lindsley reported in the vicinity of Foxpark became a fire that for a time threatened the settlement
March 1922 notice: women would no longer be employed as lookout observers in the region, citing isolation and supply problems
July 1922 Forest Service advertised for bids for a new combination fire observatory and living quarters atop the peak
Roy Last of Saratoga again stationed at Medicine Bow Peak
Arthur Strouts identified as forest lookout on Medicine Bow Peak
Photos taken September 10, 2019 show remains of the telephone line system on the peak

corrections.why: No source gives a tower height for this ground cabin site; 152.4 m (500 ft) matches nothing read. The Former Fire Lookout Sites Register gives elevation 12,009 ft (3,660 m), which agrees with elevation_m in the record.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Former Fire Lookout Sites Register gives 12,009 ft; a 1920 newspaper notice gives 12,005 ft; firelookout.com gives 12,016 ft. The story gives the register figure and the newspaper figure side by side.

A 1919 item reports a new observatory, a 1921 item says an observatory begun in 1920 would be finished that season, a July 1922 notice seeks bids for a new one, and the register says a cupola structure later replaced the cabin without a date. The story reports the dates as disagreeing and does not pick one.

notes_for_editor: Good newspaper record of staffing and fires from the Forest Lookouts page, but those clippings are secondhand transcriptions and were not checked against the newspapers. The fate is unclear: two lists say gone, and the only mention of burning is a bare caption on Forest Lookouts with no date or structure. The brief's height_m of 152.4 has no source; corrected above. The valhikes blog is outside the brief's source list; it was found by search and is a 2022 trip report, the only current-condition source. The Just Trails page is suspended (its account is closed), so its claims could not be checked. The register's Photo courtesy of American Heritage Center credit has no image URL, so no photo entry was added. The staffing notes stop at 1936; no source read says when the post ended. Access is marked public on the strength of national forest land and the 2022 trip report, not a closure or access notice.
